I01: 0/2
- Criterion 1 not met: the claimed fact says a component took almost a full second when run on its own, which denies the premise that every component finished in under half a second in those tests.
- Criterion 2 not met: the explanation depends on that denied premise, so it does not show why the whole screen could still miss the limit if each component was fast alone.
- Tip: Keep every stated test result true and weaken the leap from separate component times to the full screen.
I02: 0/2
- Criterion 1 not met: steady teenage borrowing at the other seven branches is already given in the stimulus, so it is not a new fact.
- Criterion 2 not met: the control-group explanation only restates a premise the argument already uses, rather than adding a further reason the hours caused the rise.
- Tip: Add a fact the stimulus does not already state, such as borrowing happening after 6 p.m. or no earlier upward trend.
I03: 1/2
- Criterion 1 met: a public auditor report already stating the same knowledge and six-month delay is consistent with the premises and gives a real other way to learn of the wrongdoing.
- Criterion 2 not met: the answer correctly says the “no other way” condition fails, but then infers that the code therefore forbids publishing, which the rule does not say.
- Tip: Stop at why a condition of the “publish whenever” rule is not met; do not treat non-application as a ban.
I04: 1/2
- Criterion 1 met: concentrating the drop on blocks in camera range, with little change outside that range on the same streets, is a new fact that makes the cameras a likelier cause.
- Criterion 2 not met: saying it “helps the council’s case” does not explain why a local drop, rather than a streetwide one, ties the decline to the cameras.
- Tip: Spell out the link, for example that an effect limited to camera range is what the cameras would produce and a streetwide change would not.
